title: Waylon Jennings
wiki_lead:
Waylon Arnold Jennings (born Wayland Arnold Jennings, June 15, 1937 – February 13, 2002) was an American country music singer, songwriter, musician, actor, and author. He is considered one of the pioneers of the outlaw movement in country music.
Jennings started playing guitar at age eight and performed at 14 on KVOW radio, after which he formed his first band, the Texas Longhorns. Jennings left high school at age 16, determined to become a musician, and worked as a performer and DJ on KVOW, KDAV, KYTI, KLLL, in Coolidge, Arizona, and Phoenix. In 1958, Buddy Holly arranged Jennings's first recording session, a cover of "Jole Blon", and hired him to play bass. Jennings gave up his seat on the ill-fated airplane flight in 1959 that crashed and killed Holly, J. P. "the Big Bopper" Richardson and Ritchie Valens.
Jennings then returned to Texas, taking several years off from music before eventually moving to Arizona and forming a rockabilly club band, the Waylors, which became the house band at JD's, a club in Tempe, Arizona. He recorded for independent label Trend Records and A&M Records, but did not achieve success until moving to RCA Victor in 1965. In 1972 he hired Neil Reshen as his manager, who negotiated significantly better touring and recording contracts. After Jennings gained creative control from RCA Records, he released the critically acclaimed albums Lonesome, On'ry and Mean and Honky Tonk Heroes, followed by the hit albums Dreaming My Dreams featuring number-one hit "Are You Sure Hank Done It This Way" and Are You Ready for the Country.
During the 1970s, Jennings drove outlaw country. With Willie Nelson, Tompall Glaser, and Jessi Colter he recorded country music's first platinum album, Wanted! The Outlaws. It was followed by another platinum album, a first for any solo artist in country music, Ol' Waylon, and the hit song "Luckenbach, Texas". He was featured on the 1978 album White Mansions, performed by various artists documenting the lives of Confederate Southerners during the Civil War. He appeared in films and television series, including Sesame Street and a stint as the Balladeer on The Dukes of Hazzard, composing and singing its theme song and narrating the show.
Jennings struggled with cocaine addiction, which he overcame in 1984. Later, he joined the country supergroup the Highwaymen with Willie Nelson, Kris Kristofferson, and Johnny Cash, which released three albums between 1985 and 1995. During that period, Jennings released the successful album Will the Wolf Survive. He has been named as one of the innovators of progressive country.
Jennings toured less after 1997 to spend more time with his family. Between 1999 and 2001, health problems limited his appearances. In 2001, he was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame. In 2007, he was posthumously awarded the Cliffie Stone Pioneer Award by the Academy of Country Music presented by Weylon Hofacket.

grok_lead: Waylon Jennings (June 15, 1937 â February 13, 2002) was an American country music singer, songwriter, musician, and actor renowned for pioneering the outlaw country movement in the 1970s, which emphasized artistic independence and a raw, rock-influenced sound diverging from Nashville's traditional establishment style. Born in Littlefield, Texas, to a family of modest means, Jennings rose from West Texas poverty to become a defining figure in country music, achieving 16 number-one singles on the Billboard Hot Country Songs chart, including " Good Hearted Woman " and " Luckenbach, Texas," and collaborating with icons like Willie Nelson, Johnny Cash, and Jessi Colter. Standing at 6 ft 0Â½ in (184 cm), he was known for his imposing stage presence alongside his signature baritone voice and black hat. Jennings's early life was marked by a passion for music that began in childhood; he learned guitar before age 10 and by his late teens was working as a disc jockey on Lubbock's KLLL radio station, where he met Buddy Holly in 1958. He dropped out of high school in the tenth grade and immersed himself in the local music scene, eventually playing bass for Holly's band, the Crickets, and producing his first single, "Jole Blon," under Holly's guidance in 1958. Tragically, Jennings gave up his plane seat to Holly for the fateful "Winter Dance Party" tour in 1959, surviving the crash that killed his mentor and two other music pioneers, J. P. Richardson and Ritchie Valens. After Holly's death, Jennings continued performing in Arizona and formed his own band, but his career breakthrough came in 1965 when he moved to Nashville, signed with RCA Records under producer Chet Atkins, and scored his first hit with "(Stop the World) And Let Me Off," which reached #16. In Nashville, Jennings initially chafed against the Music Row system's rigid production style, rooming with Johnny Cash and forging a rebellious path that culminated in the outlaw country era. Key albums like Lonesome, On'ry and Mean (1973) and Honky Tonk Heroes (1973) showcased his gritty baritone and songwriting, while the 1976 compilation Wanted! The Outlaws âfeaturing Nelson, Colter, and Tompall Glaserâbecame the first platinum-certified album in country music history. His duets with Nelson, such as "Mammas Don't Let Your Babies Grow Up to Be Cowboys," earned a Grammy Award for Best Country Vocal Performance by a Duo or Group in 1978, and he later formed the supergroup the Highwaymen with Nelson, Cash, and Kris Kristofferson in 1985. Jennings also narrated the theme song for the television series The Dukes of Hazzard from 1979 to 1985, broadening his cultural impact. Throughout his life, Jennings battled personal demons, including a severe cocaine addiction that peaked at $1,500 per day in the 1970s before he quit cold turkey in 1984; he was married four times, most notably to singer Jessi Colter from 1969 until his death, with whom he had a son, Shooter Jennings. Who had been diagnosed with diabetes in 1981, he underwent heart bypass surgery in 1988 and had his left foot amputated in December 2001 due to circulatory problems; he retired from touring in 2000 but continued recording until his death from diabetes-related complications on February 13, 2002, in Chandler, Arizona. Inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2001, Jennings's legacy endures as a symbol of authenticity and defiance in American music.
